answer.recommendation: Failure is not necessary for hypertrophy: when sets are equated, stopping short of failure produced similar muscle size gains to training to failure [1]. Getting close to failure may still add a small benefit, so staying near failure is reasonable [2].
answer.why: A high-grade meta-analysis of 15 randomized studies (n=394) found similar muscle size gains with failure and non-failure training when set number was equated (SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.30), with no difference by experience [3]. A trial in 42 experienced lifters agreed (6.1% vs 5.8%, p=0.74) [4]. A larger meta-analysis of 55 randomized studies (n=1326) found gains were larger as sets ended closer to failure (SMD -0.04 per repetition in reserve, 95% CI -0.07 to -0.01) [2]. A trial in 46 experienced lifters found 7.4% vs 4.9% quadriceps growth favoring failure (p=0.01) [5]. The evidence conflicts and the trials are small, so confidence is moderate, and the per-repetition effect is small [2].

positions.stance: Stopping sets short of failure produces similar muscle growth to training to failure, so failure is not necessary
positions.best_counterargument: A larger meta-analysis of 55 randomized studies (n=1326) found muscle size gains were larger as sets ended closer to failure (SMD -0.04 per repetition in reserve, 95% CI -0.07 to -0.01), and a trial in 46 experienced lifters found quadriceps growth of 7.4% with failure versus 4.9% when stopping three repetitions short (p=0.01).

positions.stance: Sets taken closer to failure produce somewhat more muscle growth, so training near or to failure is advantageous for hypertrophy
positions.best_counterargument: A meta-analysis of 15 randomized studies (n=394) found similar muscle size gains with failure and non-failure training when sets were equated (SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.30), and a 42-lifter trial in experienced trainees found 6.1% versus 5.8% vastus lateralis growth (p=0.74). The per-repetition effect in the larger meta-analysis is also small.

answer.what_would_change_this: Larger trials in experienced lifters that directly compare failure with stopping short at equal sets would settle the split between the two meta-analyses [1][2]. If you find that training to failure leaves you unable to keep your weekly sets up, that would favor stopping short.
answer.applies_to_you: As an intermediate lifter aiming for hypertrophy, the meta-analysis found no difference by experience level, so the finding should apply to you [3]. The two trials in experienced lifters disagree with each other, so the answer for trained people is not unanimous [4][5].
answer.practical_protocol: Next week, end most sets close to failure, and use failure occasionally, for example on the last set of an exercise. Keep the number of sets the same whichever way you train, since the similar results with failure and non-failure training came from equated set number [1]. Weekly set volume also matters, with each additional weekly set per muscle associated with a 0.37% increase in muscle size [6].
answer.whats_new: The 2023 meta-analysis of 55 studies (n=1326) adds a small dose-response favoring sets closer to failure, which qualifies the earlier 2021 finding of no significant difference [2][1].
answer.disclaimer: This is general, evidence-based training and nutrition information, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before making changes if you have a health condition, injury, or take medication.

verdict.rationale: The decisive evidence is two high-grade meta-analyses that do not fully agree. output.rationale: The decisive evidence is two high-grade meta-analyses that do not fully agree. The 2021 meta-analysis (15 RCTs, n=394) found no significant difference between failure and non-failure when sets were equated (SMD 0.12, CI -0.06 to 0.30), with no difference by training experience. The 2022 RCT in 42 experienced lifters agreed (6.1% vs 5.8%, p=0.74). The 2023 meta-analysis (55 studies, n=1326) found a small dose-response favoring sets closer to failure (SMD -0.04 per RIR, CI -0.07 to -0.01), and a 2024 RCT in 46 experienced lifters found 7.4% vs 4.9% favoring failure (p=0.01). P2 is right that there is a small advantage to getting close to failure. That per-rep effect is tiny, its CI nearly touches zero, and it describes proximity rather than a requirement for failure. The studies of experienced lifters are split, so the picture is not unanimous. The balance still supports P1: failure is not required, but nearer is slightly better. Confidence is moderate because the evidence conflicts and the trials are small.
